story: Listen. That is real wind, on Mars. Perseverance recorded it on its fourth day there.
One day, a person will stand in that wind. Earth will be eleven light-minutes away. If something goes wrong out there, no one can reach them in time.
Everything they need to know already exists. But it is scattered across dozens of missions, archives and formats. No single map brings it together.
So we built one. Homeward. A map of Mars made only from real data, that plans your walk, and always brings you home.
The whole planet, in true three D, from NASA and ESA orbiters. Olympus Mons. Valles Marineris. Two thousand named places, one search away.
Every place we have landed, from Mars 3 in 1971, to Zhurong. Opportunity's forty-five kilometre drive, traced from NASA's own records.
Lay the science on top: the geology, the heat of the ground, the dust. Every layer names where it came from.
Then stand where the rovers stood, and look all around, in their own photographs.
Now it is your turn. Sol one eighty two. You want to reach the rock where Curiosity found an ancient lake. First, the briefing: daylight, radiation, and what Curiosity measured there.
Homeward plans the route. It steers around slopes and rocks a suit cannot cross, and keeps air, power, dose and daylight in budget, with enough left to walk back.
Then you walk it. Every step, the display shows the way home, the air you have left, and whether your radio still reaches the habitat.
Ask the suit assistant, and it answers only with real numbers, and where they came from.
Above you, the real orbiters pass overhead, exactly where they are right now.
Every number you saw is real. Measured, computed, and cited. No demo data. Nothing invented.
Homeward. So the first people on Mars can always find their way home.
